title: Apply a type 1 diabetes sick-day plan
stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has influenza and poor appetite. They plan to stop both basal and mealtime insulin until eating normally. What needs clarification first?
options: Whether all glucose checks can wait until normal meals resume
Whether the client can simply use yesterday's mealtime doses
Whether the client should exercise whenever glucose rises
How to maintain necessary insulin and monitor during illness
why: Illness increases the need for monitoring rather than justifying a pause.
Changed intake and illness require the prescribed adjustment plan.
Exercise is not an appropriate substitute for insulin during acute illness.
Basal insulin deficiency can precipitate ketoacidosis even when intake is poor.
takeaway: Basal insulin deficiency can precipitate ketoacidosis even when intake is poor.
learningObjective: Maintain an individualized insulin and monitoring plan during illness with poor intake.

title: Address lipohypertrophy before dose escalation
stem: A client has erratic glucose despite prescribed insulin use. They inject into the same firm abdominal lump because it hurts less. What is the most useful next step?
options: Assess injection sites and teach rotation into healthy tissue
Request an immediate dose increase based only on high readings
Switch every dose to a different body region without a plan
Teach deeper injections into the same lump
why: Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and needs correction before assuming dose failure.
Increasing insulin without addressing absorption may increase subsequent hypoglycemia risk.
Unsystematic changes can add variation in absorption and make patterns harder to interpret.
Changing depth does not restore normal absorption in damaged tissue.
takeaway: Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and needs correction before assuming dose failure.
learningObjective: Address injection-site lipohypertrophy before assuming the prescribed insulin dose is ineffective.

title: Explain why insulin pens are individual devices
stem: Two spouses use the same insulin product and ask to share a pen with separate needles. What is the best explanation?
options: Cleaning the outer pen permits sharing
Blood contamination may occur inside the pen
Sharing is acceptable when neither has a known infection
Sharing is acceptable if both prescribed doses match
why: External cleaning does not disinfect its internal fluid pathway.
Changing the needle does not make a pen safe for another person.
Unrecognized bloodborne infection still makes shared use unsafe.
Matching doses does not address contamination inside the device.
takeaway: Changing the needle does not make a pen safe for another person.
learningObjective: Explain why changing needles does not make insulin pens safe to share.

title: Verify a concentrated insulin transition
stem: A client's insulin prescription changes to a concentrated pen. They want to withdraw the insulin using their old syringe because it feels familiar. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to calculate the conversion from memory
Use the old pen's appearance to identify equivalent settings
Verify the product-specific administration method and reteach with demonstration
Use the same syringe volume as the previous product
why: Device-specific safety should not rely on an improvised home conversion.
Appearance cannot establish product or delivery equivalence.
Transferring concentrated insulin to an unsuitable syringe can cause major dosing error.
Different concentrations contain different amounts in the same volume.
takeaway: Transferring concentrated insulin to an unsuitable syringe can cause major dosing error.
learningObjective: Verify device-specific administration when a concentrated insulin product is prescribed.

title: Link a sulfonylurea to skipped-meal symptoms
stem: A client taking gliclazide reports shakiness during a shift after missing lunch. They have a glucose meter available. What should the nurse advise first?
options: Wait until dinner because the morning dose has already passed
Skip tomorrow's dose and continue today's shift without assessment
Treat only if the client loses consciousness
Check glucose and follow the prescribed low-glucose plan if needed
why: Its glucose-lowering effect can persist beyond the morning meal.
A future medication change does not address the current symptoms.
Waiting permits a potentially manageable episode to become severe.
Gliclazide can cause hypoglycemia, especially when food intake is missed.
takeaway: Gliclazide can cause hypoglycemia, especially when food intake is missed.
learningObjective: Assess possible sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycemia after a missed meal.

title: Review metformin during acute renal decline
stem: A client taking metformin is admitted with vomiting, dehydration and new acute kidney injury. A usual dose is due. What is appropriate?
options: Seek prompt medication review before administering the dose
Give it because the long-term prescription has not changed
Give half the dose without contacting the team
Give it with food and defer the kidney result
why: Acute renal impairment and dehydration can change metformin safety.
The acute illness changes the assessment required before administration.
An arbitrary reduction is not an authorized renal-adjustment plan.
Food does not remove the accumulation concern from acute renal impairment.
takeaway: Acute renal impairment and dehydration can change metformin safety.
learningObjective: Reassess metformin safety when dehydration and acute renal impairment develop.

title: Recognize possible euglycemic ketoacidosis
stem: A client taking empagliflozin has persistent vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing. Glucose is only moderately elevated. What should the nurse do?
options: Give an extra empagliflozin dose for the elevated glucose
Arrange urgent assessment including consideration of ketoacidosis
Use the glucose value to exclude a diabetic emergency
Encourage oral fluid intake and review at the next clinic visit
why: Further dosing is not an appropriate response to possible ketoacidosis.
SGLT2-related ketoacidosis may occur without extreme glucose elevation.
Glucose alone cannot rule out ketoacidosis in this context.
The breathing pattern and persistent symptoms require timely acute assessment.
takeaway: SGLT2-related ketoacidosis may occur without extreme glucose elevation.
learningObjective: Recognize ketoacidosis warning symptoms during SGLT2 therapy despite modest glucose elevation.

title: Evaluate severe symptoms during GLP-1 therapy
stem: A client taking semaglutide reports severe persistent upper abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. Mild nausea had occurred previously. What is best?
options: Delay one meal and continue the dose escalation schedule
Wait to report until symptoms have lasted a full week
Arrange prompt clinical assessment before the next dose
Repeat the prior advice to eat smaller meals only
why: Continuing escalation before assessment may worsen an unresolved complication.
Persistence and severity already justify assessment.
Severe persistent pain requires evaluation beyond expected mild gastrointestinal intolerance.
Dietary advice alone is insufficient for this change in severity.
takeaway: Severe persistent pain requires evaluation beyond expected mild gastrointestinal intolerance.
learningObjective: Distinguish severe persistent abdominal symptoms from mild expected GLP-1 intolerance.

title: Assess hyperglycemia after glucocorticoids
stem: A client starts systemic prednisone and subsequently has thirst and repeatedly elevated glucose despite no prior diabetes diagnosis. What interpretation best guides care?
options: A previous normal glucose rules out a medication contribution
The client must have permanently lost all insulin production
Thirst is sufficient evidence to reduce prednisone independently
The steroid may have increased glucose and monitoring needs
why: Normal pretreatment values do not exclude steroid-associated hyperglycemia.
This presentation does not establish irreversible pancreatic failure.
Treatment changes require review of the indication and glucose management plan.
Glucocorticoids can raise glucose even without previously diagnosed diabetes.
takeaway: Glucocorticoids can raise glucose even without previously diagnosed diabetes.
learningObjective: Connect new hyperglycemia with systemic glucocorticoid exposure and monitoring needs.

title: Verify practical insulin readiness
stem: An older adult is preparing to manage a new insulin pen independently at home. Which findings support readiness? Select all that apply.
options: The client accurately demonstrates selecting and delivering the prescribed dose
The client explains when and how to treat low glucose
The client agrees with every instruction but cannot show dose selection
The client identifies the pen only by cap colour
The client relies on a family member who will not be present
why: Return demonstration tests practical ability rather than verbal agreement.
Recognizing and responding to hypoglycemia supports safer independent use.
Agreement alone does not demonstrate the ability to administer insulin.
Colour cannot reliably establish the prescribed insulin product.
A plan dependent on unavailable assistance does not support independent use.
takeaway: Return demonstration tests practical ability rather than verbal agreement.
learningObjective: Evaluate demonstrated insulin administration and hypoglycemia-management competence.

title: Plan discontinuation after prolonged steroid use
stem: A client has taken systemic prednisone daily for months and wants to stop because symptoms improved. What is the best response?
options: Continue indefinitely because tapering is never possible
Arrange a prescriber-directed taper and discuss adrenal suppression
Stop when the current package is finished regardless of dose
Alternate full doses and no doses based on daily symptoms
why: Discontinuation may be possible with an individualized monitored plan.
Prolonged therapy can suppress endogenous cortisol, making abrupt withdrawal hazardous.
Package completion does not establish a safe discontinuation schedule.
An improvised schedule does not address adrenal recovery reliably.
takeaway: Prolonged therapy can suppress endogenous cortisol, making abrupt withdrawal hazardous.
learningObjective: Explain the need for a supervised discontinuation plan after prolonged systemic steroid use.

title: Improve levothyroxine administration consistency
stem: A client takes levothyroxine with iron on some mornings and without breakfast on others. Thyroid results have become variable. What is the best teaching focus?
options: Take all missed tablets with the next iron dose
Request a higher dose before addressing administration technique
Use consistent instructed timing and separate interacting supplements
Adjust the tablet dose to each morning's energy level
why: Unreviewed catch-up and iron interaction can further destabilize exposure.
Correcting inconsistent administration may prevent unnecessary dose escalation.
Variable food and iron exposure can alter levothyroxine absorption.
Daily symptoms cannot safely determine replacement dosing.
takeaway: Variable food and iron exposure can alter levothyroxine absorption.
learningObjective: Address inconsistent levothyroxine absorption from variable meals and interacting supplements.

title: Recognize possible thyroid overreplacement
stem: After a levothyroxine increase, a client develops palpitations, heat intolerance and tremor. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend taking it later in the day without reporting
Explain that these symptoms must occur before benefit
Advise reducing food intake to control the symptoms
Report symptoms for thyroid and cardiovascular assessment
why: Timing alone does not address potentially excessive hormone exposure.
Palpitations and tremor are not required signs of successful replacement.
Dietary restriction does not correct excessive thyroid hormone effect.
The temporal pattern suggests possible overreplacement requiring review.
takeaway: The temporal pattern suggests possible overreplacement requiring review.
learningObjective: Identify possible thyroid overreplacement from new symptoms after a dose increase.

title: Report fever during antithyroid treatment
stem: A client taking methimazole develops fever and a sore throat. They ask whether to treat it as a usual cold. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly contact the treatment team for assessment and blood-count guidance
Use cold remedies and report only if symptoms persist a week
Continue monitoring thyroid symptoms without discussing the fever
Treat it as an allergy solely because fever followed treatment
why: Agranulocytosis is uncommon but serious and must be considered.
Delayed assessment may miss a serious drug-associated infection risk.
Thyroid symptom control does not exclude marrow toxicity.
Fever and sore throat require evaluation rather than an assumed mechanism.
takeaway: Agranulocytosis is uncommon but serious and must be considered.
learningObjective: Escalate fever and sore throat during methimazole therapy for marrow-toxicity assessment.

title: Evaluate oral bisphosphonate suitability
stem: A client prescribed oral alendronate cannot remain upright because of an acute back condition. What should the nurse do before administration?
options: Crush it into a small volume of food
Clarify an appropriate treatment plan or alternative
Give it with breakfast to protect the esophagus
Give it just before sleep to minimize discomfort
why: Changing formulation does not establish safety and can increase irritation.
Upright positioning is part of reducing esophageal injury with oral alendronate.
Food reduces absorption and does not replace positioning requirements.
Recumbency increases the risk of esophageal exposure.
takeaway: Upright positioning is part of reducing esophageal injury with oral alendronate.
learningObjective: Clarify oral bisphosphonate suitability when upright positioning is not possible.

title: Recognize desmopressin-associated water retention
stem: A client taking desmopressin drinks unusually large amounts of water and develops headache, confusion and weight gain. What is the priority concern?
options: An expected adaptation requiring no laboratory review
A need for an additional dose because headache persists
Water retention with possible hyponatremia
Insufficient desmopressin causing dehydration
why: New neurological symptoms require prompt assessment.
Further antidiuretic effect could worsen water retention.
Antidiuretic action plus excess intake can dilute sodium and affect the brain.
Weight gain and high intake favour water retention rather than untreated water loss.
takeaway: Antidiuretic action plus excess intake can dilute sodium and affect the brain.
learningObjective: Recognize neurological warning symptoms of water retention during desmopressin therapy.

title: Escalate failed oral adrenal replacement
stem: A client with adrenal insufficiency cannot keep prescribed hydrocortisone down during gastroenteritis and feels increasingly weak. What is appropriate?
options: Wait until the next routine tablet time
Take smaller bites of food before retrying for several hours
Replace the missed medicine with extra salt and water
Urgently follow the emergency sick-day replacement plan
why: Delay can allow adrenal crisis to develop.
A prolonged trial of oral intake can delay necessary parenteral replacement.
Fluids and salt cannot replace deficient glucocorticoid activity.
Vomiting can prevent absorption when illness increases cortisol needs.
takeaway: Vomiting can prevent absorption when illness increases cortisol needs.
learningObjective: Activate emergency replacement planning when vomiting prevents oral glucocorticoid absorption.

title: Prepare for new exercise with insulin
stem: An insulin-treated client plans to start prolonged evening exercise. Which elements belong in a safe individualized plan? Select all that apply.
options: Continue exercising through shakiness until a planned break
Monitor glucose around activity and afterward as instructed
Keep rapid carbohydrate readily available
Assume an adequate pre-exercise meal prevents every low
Omit all basal insulin on exercise days
why: Symptoms require timely assessment rather than continued exertion.
Exercise can alter glucose during activity and later recovery.
Accessible treatment supports a prompt response to low glucose.
Delayed hypoglycemia can still occur despite prior food intake.
Blanket basal omission can create significant insulin deficiency.
takeaway: Exercise can alter glucose during activity and later recovery.
learningObjective: Plan glucose monitoring and hypoglycemia treatment around a new exercise pattern.

title: Plan insulin use across time zones
stem: A client using basal and mealtime insulin will cross several time zones. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use home-clock timing for every dose without reviewing meal changes
Pack all insulin with ice directly against the cartridges
Estimate new doses after arrival based only on hunger
Obtain an individualized dosing and monitoring schedule
Carry accessible supplies and hypoglycemia treatment
why: Rigid timing may mismatch local meals and dose intervals.
Freezing can damage insulin and make it unreliable.
Hunger is not an adequate measure of insulin requirements.
Time changes can alter intervals between doses and meals.
Lost checked luggage should not interrupt essential treatment.
takeaway: Time changes can alter intervals between doses and meals.
learningObjective: Prepare an individualized insulin schedule for travel across time zones.

title: Evaluate emergency glucagon teaching
stem: A partner receives training with the client's prescribed glucagon rescue device. Which statement shows appropriate understanding?
options: I will try to give a drink before using it even if swallowing is unsafe
I will practise by partly discharging the real rescue device
I will use the device as taught and call for emergency help
If the person wakes, no further glucose checks are needed
why: Oral intake during impaired consciousness creates aspiration risk.
A partially used single-use device may not provide the intended emergency dose.
Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue treatment plus assessment and continued monitoring.
Low glucose can recur and the cause still needs review.
takeaway: Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue treatment plus assessment and continued monitoring.
learningObjective: Evaluate a caregiver's understanding of prescribed glucagon rescue and subsequent monitoring.

title: Assess abnormal insulin appearance
stem: A clear insulin product now contains visible particles after being left near a heater. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use it if the next glucose reading is normal
Increase the dose to compensate for possible loss of potency
Refrigerate it again and assume potency is restored
Do not use it and arrange a verified replacement
why: A glucose result cannot verify the damaged product's reliability.
The degree of damage is unknown, making dose compensation unsafe.
Cooling cannot reverse damage already caused by improper storage.
Unexpected particles and heat exposure raise concern about product integrity.
takeaway: Unexpected particles and heat exposure raise concern about product integrity.
learningObjective: Respond to abnormal insulin appearance after possible heat damage.

title: Respond to interrupted pump delivery
stem: A client with type 1 diabetes finds that insulin pump delivery stopped several hours ago. They feel well but glucose is rising. What should happen?
options: Check glucose and ketones as directed and activate the backup insulin plan
Wait for symptoms before using the backup plan
Give a correction through the same unverified malfunctioning system
Reconnect and postpone all monitoring until bedtime
why: Pump interruption can quickly lead to insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
Feeling well does not exclude evolving insulin deficiency.
The intended dose may not be delivered until function is confirmed.
Restored connection alone does not show that glucose and ketones are safe.
takeaway: Pump interruption can quickly lead to insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
learningObjective: Activate a backup insulin plan when pump interruption causes rising glucose.

title: Distinguish antithyroid benefit from excessive suppression
stem: A client starts treatment for hyperthyroidism. Which change best supports the intended response?
options: The client reports a new sore throat and fever
Resting tachycardia and tremor decrease without new cold intolerance
Weight rises rapidly with profound lethargy and cold intolerance
Palpitations persist but the client is less worried
why: These can indicate an important adverse effect requiring assessment.
This suggests reduced excess hormone effect without clear hypothyroid symptoms.
These findings may suggest excessive suppression rather than balanced treatment.
Reduced anxiety does not establish a physiological treatment response.
takeaway: This suggests reduced excess hormone effect without clear hypothyroid symptoms.
learningObjective: Distinguish controlled hyperthyroidism from excessive suppression or treatment toxicity.

title: Clarify an incomplete correction scale
stem: A client's premeal glucose lies above the highest range on the prescribed insulin correction scale. The client is alert and the meal is available. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the highest listed dose as the final plan
Withhold all insulin and omit repeat glucose testing
Contact the authorized prescriber or follow the escalation instruction
Extend the scale by repeating its last numerical increment
why: That dose may be insufficient or inappropriate for the unlisted range.
Uncertainty about one dose does not remove ongoing assessment needs.
The incomplete scale does not authorize extrapolation to an unlisted range.
A pattern in listed doses is not a prescription for higher values.
takeaway: The incomplete scale does not authorize extrapolation to an unlisted range.
learningObjective: Seek an authorized dose when a correction scale omits the current glucose range.

title: Recognize complications during chronic corticosteroid therapy
stem: A client taking long-term systemic corticosteroids is reviewing when to call the clinic. Which findings need prompt reporting? Select all that apply.
options: New fever with a worsening cough
Black sticky stools with new light-headedness
Joint pain improves enough to walk farther
The prescribed morning administration routine remains consistent
Mild appetite improvement without other changes
why: Immunosuppression raises concern about infection and its progression.
This pattern may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding.
Functional improvement may be an intended anti-inflammatory benefit.
Consistent timing alone is not evidence of a complication.
This can occur with corticosteroids and is less urgent than the listed red flags.
takeaway: Immunosuppression raises concern about infection and its progression.
learningObjective: Identify infection and bleeding warning symptoms during chronic systemic corticosteroid use.
